## What it is

Gelman found this saying attributed to him online and couldn't remember saying it, so he asked his readers. A commenter traced it to his own talk "Theoretical Statistics is the Theory of Applied Statistics: How to Think About What We Do" at the 2017 New York R Conference: "Computer programing is basically the last bastion of rigor in the modern world. I don't trust anything until it runs. In fact, until it runs twice on the computer."

The post doesn't explain the second run. Our reading: code that runs once might have worked by luck: a lucky random seed, an initial value that happened to fall in the right place, a cached object from an earlier session. Running it a second time, from a fresh start, a different seed or a different initialization, tests whether the result is a property of the problem or of that particular run.

## Why it matters

In statistical computing this matters a great deal. MCMC with a single chain can't tell you whether it explored the whole posterior. An optimizer started once can't tell you whether it found the global optimum. A notebook run once can't tell you whether it depends on hidden state. Running more than once, with multiple chains, multiple starting points or a clean environment, is the cheapest diagnostic there is.

## How it works

Take a posterior with two separated modes. A sampler started near one mode may stay there for the whole run and report a confident, unimodal answer. A second chain, started elsewhere, lands in the other mode. The disagreement between runs is the diagnostic: R-hat across chains turns "runs twice" into a number.

## Simulated example

A Metropolis sampler on a bimodal posterior. Run it once and then twice, from different random starting points, and compare.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
import {rng, range, mean, dnorm, fmt} from "../js/stats.js"
```

```{ojs}
viewof gap = Inputs.range([1, 8], {value: 5, step: 0.25, label: "Distance between the two modes"})
viewof step = Inputs.range([0.1, 3], {value: 0.5, step: 0.1, label: "Proposal step size"})
viewof seed = Inputs.range([1, 500], {value: 1, step: 1, label: "Random seed"})
```

```{ojs}
twice = {
  const r = rng(seed);
  const logp = x => Math.log(0.5 * dnorm(x, -gap / 2, 0.7) + 0.5 * dnorm(x, gap / 2, 0.7) + 1e-300);
  const run = (start, label) => {
    let x = start, lp = logp(x);
    return range(2000).map(t => {
      const y = x + r.normal(0, step), ly = logp(y);
      if (Math.log(r()) < ly - lp) { x = y; lp = ly; }
      return {t, x, label};
    });
  };
  return [...run(r.uniform(-gap, gap), "Run 1"), ...run(r.uniform(-gap, gap), "Run 2")];
}
```

```{ojs}
Plot.plot({
  ariaLabel: "Until it runs twice: simulation chart",
  ariaDescription: "Horizontal axis: Iteration. Vertical axis: Draw. The chart updates with the controls above it, and the summary below the charts states the result in words.",
  height: 280,
  x: {label: "Iteration"},
  y: {label: "Draw", grid: true},
  color: {legend: true, range: ["#2166ac", "#d6604d"]},
  marks: [Plot.line(twice, {x: "t", y: "x", stroke: "label", strokeWidth: 0.7})]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const m = l => mean(twice.filter(d => d.label === l && d.t >= 1000).map(d => d.x));
  const differ = Math.abs(m("Run 1") - m("Run 2")) > 1;
  return html`<div class="sim-readout">${md`Second-half means: run 1 **${fmt(m("Run 1"))}**, run 2 **${fmt(m("Run 2"))}**. The true posterior mean is 0. ${differ ? "The two runs disagree. Either one alone would have given a confident, wrong answer. Running twice exposed it." : "This time the runs agree. Try other seeds or a bigger gap. Agreement across runs is what earns trust."}`}</div>`;
}
```

## Key takeaways

::: takeaways
- One successful run proves little. Run again from a different starting point.
- Multiple MCMC chains, multiple initializations and clean environments are cheap and catch a lot.
- If the answer changes between runs, the answer isn't known yet.
:::
